accuracy.evidence: Matches the PSHE Association programme of study KS1 L1 (what rules are, why they are needed, and why different rules are needed for different situations), the non-statutory KS1 PSHE and citizenship framework 2d (agree and follow rules for their group and classroom, and understand how rules help them), DfE (2019) Relationships Education guidance on fairness and respect, and CASEL responsible decision-making. Reasons are kept to the three widely taught purposes: safety, fairness and working together.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the known errors at 5 to 7: rules only count when an adult watches (look-away step, p3, m4, 'watch' challenge tag), rules have no reason or are just bossy ('nowhy' tag, adult text on 'because I said so'), no rules is more fun ('fun' tag, m1, chaos scenes), fair means I get my way ('unfair' tag, agreement faces, m2) and the same rules apply everywhere ('same' tag, place step, m5).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagwhyrule is new: a reason sorter with Safe, Fair and Together jars, animated no-rule scenes (slide, hall, tag) where children wander and bump until the right rule is dropped and they line up, a look-away scene with the grown-up shown not looking, an agreement builder where every child face turns happy or sad, and a place matcher. Top shingle similarity is 7.0% (flag_sva.js), well below 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step makes the child act on the idea: find the reason for 3 rules, fix 3 rule-less places, choose 3 times while nobody is watching, make 3 agreements that every face accepts, and match 3 rules to places. Wrong drops explain why in one sentence (for example 'Sorry does not stop the bump. Walking does.'), so the reason, not the rule, is what is learned.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions come before the action: what happens at a slide where nobody takes turns, whether class rules count when the teacher goes out, and whether shouting fine at football is fine in the library. A.reveal reports the child's guess back against what they then see in the scene.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions rotate answer order, and every wrong choice is tagged (watch, fun, unfair, nowhy, same) with its own fix sentence, e.g. 'The reason does not go away when nobody is looking. Keep the rule anyway.' Correct answers build a stars-in-a-row streak and the Another button gives a fresh question.

readability.evidence: Kid text grades at FK 1.6 with short sentences and everyday words (slide, swing, tag, biscuit); adult text grades at FK 6.9. Lab text uses very simple words for ages 5 to 7 with one idea per line, and every scene has an emoji picture of the children, place or grown-up so meaning does not rely on reading.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph does a job: kid text gives the reason for rules, the no-rules game, agreements and place rules; adult text gives curriculum framing, two named mistakes (rules only as orders, fair as getting my way) with what to say instead, and what the lab does. The family tip is a concrete activity: make one family agreement and ask 'what was our reason?'.

mobile.evidence: Canvas uses the tall ratio on narrow screens, option rows are 46 px or more high and full width, sort jars span the screen width, and every drag has a big button twin below the canvas, so the whole lab works by tapping on an iPhone 13. Walkthrough checked on desktop and iPhone 13 in light and dark themes.

accessibility.evidence: Canvas carries a live aria-label that is updated with every prompt and result, the controls group has an aria-label, the challenge feedback is a polite live region, all colours come from theme tokens so contrast holds in light and dark, the chaos animation stops under reduced motion, and axe runs clean in both themes.

sources: PSHE Association (2020) Programme of Study for PSHE Education, Key Stage 1 L1 and R20
DfE (2000) Non-statutory framework for PSHE and citizenship at key stages 1 and 2, KS1 2d
DfE (2019) Relationships Education, Relationships and Sex Education and Health Education statutory guidance
